blocks.text: He was certainly the most handsome Habsburg who ever lived. Tall, slender, with features of the noblest cut. Charming, athletic, a loving father, and some contemporaries even preferred him as heir to the Austrian throne over his own brother, Franz Ferdinand. In the family they called him “Boller.

” The public, however, remembered him differently: as the handsome archduke, the reckless husband, the scandalous playboy who ultimately died a miserable death from syphilis. Archduke Otto Franz Josef Karl Ludwig Maria was the second son of Archduke Karl Ludwig, a younger brother of Emperor Franz Joseph. His mother was Maria Annunziata of Naples-Sicily, Karl Ludwig’s second wife. Franz Ferdinand had been born in 1863.

Otto followed on April 21, 1865, in Graz, at the Palais Kuhburg. His younger siblings were Ferdinand Karl, born 1868, and Margarete Sophie, born 1870. The family spent their first years in Graz because Karl Ludwig hoped the milder climate would benefit his wife, who came from Southern Italy and had frail health. But Maria Annunziata had suffered from a severe lung disease since her youth. As her condition worsened, the family moved to Vienna so she could be treated by specialists. For the children, their mother’s illness meant a painful distance. For fear of contagion, the sons were not allowed to hug her and could barely speak to her. Karl Ludwig had Villa Wartholz built in Reichenau an der Rax, hoping the health resort would help her. That hope was never fulfilled. Maria Annunziata died in 1871, shortly after the birth of her daughter. Otto was only six. After her death, Karl Ludwig married the Portuguese Infanta Maria Theresa, who became a loving stepmother to the four half-orphans.

She developed an especially close bond with Otto, since both loved sports, horses, painting, and the then still-young art of photography. In general, Otto was extremely popular within the family. His cheerful nature, his social grace, and his ability to win people over stayed with him his whole life. He was also his father’s declared favorite, favored by his tutors as well. For Franz Ferdinand, that was certainly not easy to endure. The family lived in Vienna in the Palais Archduke Karl Ludwig on Favoritenstraße, with summer residences including Villa Wartholz and Artstetten Castle. Like Franz Ferdinand, Otto was initially a sickly child. Later, however, he developed into a better rider and a more skilled fencer than his brother. The children received an education typical for members of the Imperial House, under the supervision of Count Ferdinand von Degenfeld-Schonburg. About the young Otto, it was said that he was a real rascal and generally did not learn his lessons. He played many a prank on his teachers and was constantly up to mischief. Learning was not one of his passions.

As was customary for male members of the dynasty, he was required to learn a trade. He chose woodturning, but also worked as a joiner and carpenter. Together with his valet, he felled trees by hand. In Schönau an der Triesting, he later concerned himself with viticulture and winemaking. But then came the transition to the military. Like almost all male Habsburgs, Otto embarked on a military career. He came to Klagenfurt as a young officer in the 8th Uhlan Regiment. There he befriended First Lieutenant Baron von E. , described as a dashing cavalry officer who loved wine and women in equal measure. In that environment, the lifestyle developed that would permanently shape Otto’s reputation. He drank, partied, visited dubious establishments, and surrounded himself with officers who exploited his position or encouraged his debauchery. His social rank protected him.

What would have triggered disciplinary proceedings, dismissal, or even criminal prosecution for an ordinary soldier was covered up, paid off, or downplayed as a prank for an archduke. This caused resentment. People wondered why people were treated so unequally and how it could happen that gross cases of immorality appeared in the highest ruling house of all. In September 1887, Crown Prince Rudolf and his wife Stephanie traveled with several relatives and friends to Ort an der Donau for a deer hunt. The party included Archduke Otto, his brother Franz Ferdinand, Stephanie’s sister Louise of Coburg with her husband Philip, and a hunting friend, Count Josef Hoyos. After dinner, the famous Schrammel Quartet played, and Josef Bratfisch, a singer and virtuoso whistler, performed Viennese songs. After the ladies had retired, the songs became cruder and the conversation turned into an uninhibited stag party. The hunting companion Püchel described what followed. The Archduke returned carrying something under his coat. The moment he entered the salon, a muffled meow could be heard. “Well,” Püchel thought, “this is going to be some fun again. ” After a few minutes, the Archduke came back out and said, “I would like two or three dachshunds.

” A hunter brought three. Archduke Otto pushed the dogs through the slightly open door into the dining room. Immediately, the dogs began barking very excitedly, and soon a loud clattering caused by shattered glass and porcelain could be heard. Püchel rushed into the salon and saw an interesting sight. The cat dashed several times across the table, which was still set. The dachshunds chased after it, barking furiously from chairs to table, accompanied by the liveliest applause from the art-loving crowd, for this was exactly to their taste. The Crown Prince tried, laughing heartily, to fend off the dogs, while both archdukes spurred them on. It was a deafening noise. Finally, the sturdy cat fled onto the sideboard and from there into the crown of a deer antler, which tipped over. The cat jumped off and, using Bratfisch’s massive bald head as a springboard, landed back on the floor. Bratfisch jumped up with a scream and slapped his palms onto his head with a loud smack. When he found his hands covered in blood, he stormed out the door, holding his head, and down to the well in the courtyard to wash the blood from his scalp.

A typical amusement of the time. Or were there already people back then who did not find it funny when animals were baited for the entertainment of a drunken group and people were injured? But that was nothing compared to what followed. During a stay in Luxembourg, Otto, along with Rudolf, Franz Ferdinand, and Püchel, wanted to break into a poultry coop and steal animals. Otto asked Püchel to bring about twenty to thirty bantams, each about twenty-five centimeters long. After the archdukes had shot a few birds, Otto suggested to the Crown Prince, “Let’s make off with some of the poultry keeper’s charges. That would be a hell of a lot of fun. ” “My dearest Otto,” Rudolf replied, “you’re always ready for some mischief.

You would have to commit a break-in, as there’s no other way to get inside. But if it amuses you, then fine by me. ” Otto took command. Together with Püchel and Franz Ferdinand, he threw himself against the door of the poultry house, which finally gave way, causing the three of them to fall into the coop along with the door. A terrible squawking from the ducks ensued. Franz Ferdinand shouted, “Phew, I’ve dirtied my hands with duck muck! They smell absolutely awful. ” The Crown Prince was outside, doubled over with laughter.

After a while, the archdukes began rounding up the poultry. Püchel waited outside to tie the captured birds together in pairs. The first prize was a large white swan. While Püchel was tying up the swan, Archduke Otto suddenly let out a heart-wrenching scream, dropped the half-bound bird, and grabbed his backside. With two wild geese still in his hands, he rushed toward his brother. “But Otto, don’t yell like that. People will surely hear you as far as Mödling. You’re going to spoil all our fun. What happened, anyway? ”

“The swan bit me terribly in the backside,” Otto cried, “and tore a piece out of my trousers. Rudi, look at how the beast has mangled me — a big hole in my trousers and bitten bloody. Look at my fingers, they’re completely bloody. ” The Crown Prince could not speak for laughing. Püchel suggested disinfecting the wound, and the group stepped behind a bush. The Archduke dropped his trousers. Since the moon provided favorable lighting, the treatment of the roughly two-centimeter-long laceration was quickly completed.

Suddenly, Archduke Franz called out to his brother, “Oh Otto, don’t make such a scene with your bottom. ” “Püchel, stick a large plaster over the hole next to it, too,” Otto whispered, adding, “my brother tells such tasteful jokes. ” The men brought a total of tied-up live birds into the swimming school. There, Franz Ferdinand threw the animals over the plank, even though they hit the wall in the dark, fell stunned into the water, and drowned.

The next morning, the desperate supervisor said to Püchel, “Mr. Püchel, I tell you, I am the unhappiest man in the world and its surroundings. ” This story was no longer a harmless prank. It spoke of violence, animal cruelty, and a group of privileged men for whom property, rules, and the suffering of others apparently played little role. The escapades of the young archdukes eventually even became a political matter. The member of parliament Engelbert Pernerstorfer, initially a German nationalist and later a Social Democrat, brought up several stories in parliament about high-ranking young men. His speech went: “I am aware of a story about a very young and very high-ranking gentleman who, after a wild drinking bout with his comrades — all high-ranking gentlemen, also very young — wanted to lead these friends into his wife’s room. Furthermore, I am aware of the story of a very young, very high-ranking gentleman who, with his comrades, all of princely blood, was charging on horseback across a wide field, where they saw a funeral procession from afar, which they forced to stop, and all this noble princely blood made a sport of jumping over the coffin.

Then I am aware of another story from a city that admittedly has no university, but a cavalry barracks, where young gentlemen did something that perhaps the Minister of Education is aware of. When one presents these verified examples, known across entire crown lands, one can justifiably speak of brutalization and savagery. But this is not the bourgeois youth, not the youth of the common people. This is a very noble youth. ” Pernerstorfer named no names, yet the allusions were understood. Depending on the account, the jump over the funeral procession is attributed to Otto or Franz Ferdinand. Even Empress Elisabeth addressed the incident in a poem:

A true event occurred in town. The riders now meet the procession. Even though the path was not wider, they would have had enough room. But from his noble horse, the boss waves to the priest. He says down to the ground: “Put the priest down, you. ” He knows the noble offspring from a high house and therefore tirelessly issues orders immediately. Just set him down quickly, for as you all see, the prince will then dismount to offer a prayer. But he pulls on the reins of the noble thoroughbred, spanking him and making him light in the mouth. Then he leaps with a light bound over the coffin, lightening up to his bald spot. The priest is shrieking too harshly.

Elisabeth’s poem showed how well-known these accusations must have been, even within the family and at court. The other major scandal that Pernerstorfer addressed concerned an incident in a barracks, where a non-commissioned officer died under unexplained circumstances and for which Otto was held responsible. Shortly after Pernerstorfer’s speech, the politician was attacked and beaten by two armed men in his apartment. Suspicion immediately fell on Otto, but even Crown Prince Rudolf was now involved in the cover-up. He wrote: “The police have caused me some bad hours. They discovered the tracks and also the regiment from which the beating originated. They couldn’t find the men, because we posted one in Southern Hungary and the other in Herzegovina. It took all my audacity to save myself and Boller from it all. ”

The letter was explosive. It described not only an act of violence in which members of the ruling house were involved, but apparently also an attempt to hide the perpetrators and use the dynasty’s influence to hinder police investigations. How Otto came to his bride was also a strange story. In 1886, Emperor Franz Joseph wanted Franz Ferdinand to find a wife befitting his rank among the daughters of the Saxon royal house. Franz Ferdinand traveled to Saxony with Otto but showed no interest in any of the princesses and reportedly behaved extremely rudely. To save the embarrassing situation, twenty-one-year-old Otto asked for the hand of Princess Maria Josepha. Princess Nora Fugger later described the marriage: “The Archduke was married at the age of just 21. His father had wished it, and so, as always happened at court, two young beings were bound together for life without having gotten to know each other. Both were full of good qualities, but they were unworldly and fundamentally different in their characters. I often pitied Archduchess Maria Josepha, for she was a good, noble woman, strictly and excellently raised as a Princess of Saxony. She certainly approached the Archduke with great love. But what good did it do?

She was not the one who would have suited his nature. ” Crown Prince Rudolf had similar doubts. He wrote to Franz Ferdinand: “Otto’s engagement interested us greatly. I cannot say I am pleased, for I still consider him a bit too young, not well-traveled enough, not mature enough. He has hardly enjoyed life yet, and I do not know if she will capture his interest for the long term. I hope she is not like her sister, whom I know. The whole engagement went so quickly; he could have considered a few others. Why this hurry?

But now it is too late for all that. May God grant him happiness and contentment. ” The wedding was celebrated on October 2, 1886, in Dresden with great pomp. Thousands of schoolchildren, singers, and torchbearers took part in the tributes. The church wedding took place amidst the ringing of bells and cannon salutes. Afterward, the couple appeared to the cheering crowd on the balcony of the Royal Palace. A gala banquet, a festival performance at the Court Theater, and a final court ball concluded the multi-day festivities. But behind the magnificent facade, the prerequisites for a happy marriage were poor.

Maria Josepha had been raised strictly Catholic, and Otto loved pleasures, horses, hunts, and a life without limits. Ludwig Salvator wrote: “The jovial playboy Otto was brought in as a stopgap, and though he took Josefa home without objection, Otto continued to live as if he were single. ” In the very year of the wedding, Otto is said to have thrown portraits of the imperial couple out of a window during a carouse. Later, he reportedly attempted to lead his fellow officers into his wife’s bedroom. Empress Elisabeth combined both stories in a poem:

A true story that happened in Klagenfurt in the year 1886. Hey there, Habsburg, what is wrong? You stare hopelessly at your lap and wring your aged hands, as if your end were already near. Woe, woe, that I had to live to see this day of mourning. Woe that my womb ever bore the one who is my greatest disgrace. Old woman, stop the lamenting. Tell me instead what happened. Can nothing cure you anymore? Are the Russians already near? I am heavily pressured from the outside and surrounded by enemies on all sides. But at home, the wild lifestyle is what ruins my greatness. One of my younger sons, high in rank but low in conduct, deeper than any commoner, is the one who cut my heart today.

In the pub, such a ruckus, drinking and clinking of glasses; the example is set from above by the Archduke-officer. Tables and chairs must shatter and break into a thousand pieces. Glasses ring in shards of sound, turning everything around. Now at last you too shall fly, Emperor mine, and together with your wife lie soft in the dirt below. He speaks, and both portraits fly out the window to the mud, if the farmers haven’t lied, to the mayor’s distress. But the brutality of the drunken heroes’ band does not end here. Follow me, calls the drunken Highness, you shall truly not regret it. I will lead you home to my imperial quarters, and after our fine feast, you shall see lovely things with me. There in light nightwear lies my wife from Saxony in the great marriage bed, and believe me, she is quite nice. Into the nightly empty alleys rush the gentlemen officers. Soon, loud shouts and the clanking of spurs echo through the streets. But still, there is a brave man who protects with his own body the threatened young woman against all those wretched slaves.

Entrance to this chamber only over my dead body. I would rather die than give way; a curse upon you and your disgrace. Thus the Archduke’s adjutant swore to this last disgraceful act as a memorial page for my chronicle. The last verse was very remarkable, for here the Empress criticized not only Otto. She labeled her own dynasty as a decadent brood financed by the people. Elisabeth’s alienation from the ruling house could hardly be formulated more clearly. Near Villach, Otto and his drunken comrades once knocked over a stove and nearly started a fire. In a hotel in St. Veit, officers threw glasses, dishes, and furniture out of the window during a drinking bout. The aggrieved innkeeper presented a bill, which Otto initially indignantly rejected. Only when the innkeeper threatened a public scandal was it paid. A counselor to Franz Joseph described it in shock: Otto drank in full uniform in the most disreputable places with common prostitutes or held debauched revels in the locked rooms of various hotels.

According to him, these orgies completely overshadowed even the most shameless acts from the time of the deepest decline of the Roman Empire. One of the most famous stories takes place at the Hotel Sacher. After a drinking bout, Otto’s friends locked him out of the salon, and there stood the Archduke naked in the hallway, wearing only a saber — or, according to other versions, additionally wearing white gloves and the Order of the Golden Fleece. At that very moment, the British ambassador appeared in the company of high-ranking ladies. He filed a complaint with the Emperor, whereupon Franz Joseph placed Otto under house arrest in a monastery for two months. The imperial valet Eugen Kettel later recounted: “Otto’s stay significantly depleted the monastery’s wine reserves. ” His education, and especially his spelling, were also publicly mocked. Regarding letters that a coachman supposedly showed around in a wine tavern, it was said they described the depraved girls he ordered for himself in an unheard-of, casual manner.

The guests were horrified by the content, but no less by the fact that the Archduke had no clue about German orthography and committed spelling errors that one would not forgive a primary school student. We must, however, be cautious with reports from Countess Marie Larisch-Wallersee. She later claimed, among other things, that Otto had fed a young man schnapps until he died and had cruelly tortured animals. Larisch is indeed an important contemporary witness, but she is nonetheless a problematic source. Such grave accusations must not be presented as established facts without verification. They do, however, show the image of the Archduke that was circulating at the time: that of an unbridled, excessive person. But people are not one-dimensional. In stark contrast to these excesses, Otto was a loving father, and he was very popular with many people. Some would have even liked to see him as Emperor. Otto’s marriage to Maria Josepha produced two sons: Karl Franz Josef, born in 1887, and Maximilian Eugen, born in 1895. What no one could have guessed back then was that Otto’s firstborn would become the last Emperor of Austria. The parents’ marriage unfortunately remained unhappy.

Maria Josepha and Otto had little in common. In tradition, she always appears as very pious, socially oriented, and uninterested in horses or nature, in contrast to Otto, who was a passionate rider, hunter, and sportsman. The marriage was characterized by dynastic pressure, public humiliations of Maria Josepha, and her husband’s long absences. While Otto lived in garrisons for months and was transferred repeatedly, Maria Josepha lived with his parents or traveled alone without the children, which is why she has often been portrayed in retrospect as a cold-hearted mother. Otto, in turn, is said to have been a bad husband but an astonishingly loving father. He chose child-friendly tutors, played with Karl and Maximilian, and photographed them often. He wanted to provide them with a broad education without exposing them to excessive pressure. He furnished his frequently changing residences with great taste, employed good chefs, and carefully selected staff. In winter, he worked in his studios, painting animals and landscapes. He created a portrait of his young son Karl that he copied several times for family members. Another passion of his was thoroughbred horses. Otto bought, bred, and trained horses and entered them into well-known races.

It was said that he himself could turn a six-horse carriage in the tightest of spaces. He was a man of many interests, charming, and known for his good looks. When he visited the summer villa in Reichenau an der Rax, relatives and summer guests sought his company and invited him for tennis, tea, or dinner. Otto was particularly close friends with his cousin, Crown Prince Rudolf. Their friendship, which began in their youth, lasted until Rudolf’s death. And since their wives also got along well, the couples met frequently in Laxenburg. After the death of Crown Prince Rudolf in 1889, Otto’s father, Karl Ludwig, moved up in the line of succession. When Karl Ludwig died seven years later, his older son Franz Ferdinand became the heir to the throne. But Franz Ferdinand was suffering from a severe lung disease. He spent long periods at health resorts, and many at court believed he would not survive or would not be able to rule later on. In this situation, Otto took over representative duties for his brother. His uncomplicated manner was well received.

Emperor Franz Joseph also liked his charming nephew. Otto respected the Emperor’s rank but was apparently able to speak more freely with him than other members of the family. When Otto received the Augarten Palace in Vienna as a representative residence and his household was enlarged, rumors arose that the Emperor wanted to build him up as the future successor to the throne instead of Franz Ferdinand. Franz Ferdinand understandably reacted with hurt. On December 19, 1896, he wrote to Princess Nora Fugger: “Now all of a sudden Otto gets Augarten, a court household, a court kitchen, Lipizzaners in Vienna and in the countryside, and so on. By God, believe me, it is not envy that speaks through me. I wish good Otto, who always begs my forgiveness in tears, everything and even more. But it is a sense of justice that speaks through me, and then the feeling of how I am being perceived. I am receiving a lot of inquiries from abroad as to what it is I have done. ”

Whether Emperor Franz Joseph actually planned a formal change to the succession is another question. What is certain is that Otto was the dynastic reserve in those years. Had Franz Ferdinand died or renounced his claim, Otto would have taken his place. But Franz Ferdinand recovered. However, when he married Sophie Chotek in 1900, he had to accept that the marriage was morganatic. Sophie was not recognized as the equal wife of a future ruler, and their children were excluded from the line of succession. This meant that Otto, and his sons after him, remained in the line of succession. Otto disapproved of his brother’s morganatic marriage and, like his other siblings, stayed away from the wedding. The relationship between the brothers reached its lowest point as a result. But Otto was never to become the official heir to the throne, as his early death changed everything. Around 1900, his numerous affairs became his undoing.

Otto fell ill with syphilis. The sexually transmitted infection was not reliably curable at that time. Salvarsan was not developed until 1909 and was only used therapeutically starting in 1910. For Otto, this development came too late. Count Kielmansegg recorded the assessment of a doctor named Professor Mracek, who said he had never in his entire practice experienced such virulence of venereal poison as in the case of the poor Archduke. All his remedies failed and he was beyond saving. In July 1906, the Emperor discharged him from military service due to his illness. Otto, who apparently still hoped for recovery, complained about this in a letter to Nora Fugger. But the disease was destroying his body. His nose and larynx began to rot. For his damaged nasal skeleton, a prosthesis made of rubber was crafted, and at times he also wore a leather cover. In the last months of his life, he lived in his villa in the Vienna Cottage Quarter.

His mistress, the operetta singer Luise Robinson, nursed him. By the end, there was no contact with the imperial family whatsoever. Only his loving stepmother, Marie Therese, did not leave his side. She held his head so that the cannula in his larynx would not shift. On November 1, 1906, Otto died at the age of just 41. His wife outlived him by nearly four decades, dying in 1944 in Bavaria. Otto passed away eight years before his brother Franz Ferdinand. And when Franz Ferdinand and Sophie were murdered in Sarajevo in 1914, none of their children could become heirs to the throne, as they had been excluded. Now, Otto’s eldest son, Karl, moved to the head of the succession and would eventually even become Emperor. Cultural historian William Johnston summarized the reaction to Otto’s death as follows: when Otto died, the press indulged in effusive praise for an Archduke whom everyone knew had been a rake. Besides his two legitimate sons, this rake had fathered other children, albeit out of wedlock. From his relationship with the dancer Marie Schleinzer came a son and a daughter.

He had two more sons with Luise Robinson. After Otto’s death, she received a settlement from Franz Joseph of one hundred thousand crowns for each child. Finally, there is a conversation Otto had with Luise Robinson, which she published in 1928, providing a very personal insight into his way of thinking: “You know, Luisel, it always infuriated me that people don’t think anything of us at all. They believe we only care about women and horses, but after all, one is someone oneself. One is not entirely empty like an unfurnished apartment. Do you think any Viennese knows that I am a quite capable architect? Was I ever allowed to study for that? Did I ever take any exams?

Did I ever learn anything useful at all? They tortured me with things I didn’t understand and which I have long since forgotten. But who ever asked what I am and what gives me joy? ” Archduke Otto was only 41 years old. He remained remembered for his good looks, his charm, and above all, his scandalous lifestyle. Yet his life cannot be reduced to a few racy anecdotes. Behind the label of the “handsome Archduke” lies the story of a man who nearly reached the top of the monarchy, of a system that united its members while shielding them from responsibility, and of a public that knew of scandals but for a long time had little power to force consequences.
